scenes.caption: In 1972, a lighthouse keeper off the coast of Maine wrote his final log entry. It was not found for fifty years.
The log was routine at first. Weather. Fuel. The ships that passed in the night.
But on October 14th, the handwriting changed. It became shaky. Desperate.
There is a second light on the water, he wrote. It does not blink. It only watches.
The next entry was one sentence. It came up the stairs. I counted every one.
The final entry was written in a hand that did not look human. If you are reading this, you already know how it ends.
The Coast Guard found the tower empty. The lamp was still lit. The keeper was never found.
Last year, a diver found the log in a sealed case on the seabed, three hundred meters from shore. Someone carried it out.
And here is the part nobody can explain. The final line is dated tomorrow. Would you have kept reading? Comment LIGHT if this gave you chills.
Hikers in the Rockies call him the Mountain Man. He has lived alone up there for forty years. No one knows his real name.
Rangers tried to count how many cabins he has. They stopped counting at seven.
He leaves no tracks in winter. None. Fresh snow, and the path to his cabin stays untouched.
A college student hiked up to interview him in 2019. His footage was found three days later, still recording.
In the video, the Mountain Man seems normal. Kind, even. He offers the student tea.
Then, off camera, a voice asks a question. Not the student's voice. The student laughs and says, who else is up here with you?
The Mountain Man smiles and says, you should not have heard that.
The camera keeps running for six more hours. It only catches footsteps coming down the mountain. Never going up.
The student's family still posts about him every year. The Mountain Man has never been charged with anything. There is no body. Would you have drunk the tea?
Every city has buses you can see on a schedule. This one is not on any schedule. It only stops at 3:33 AM.
The first passenger who spoke about it was a nurse coming off a night shift.
She said the bus was warm inside, and every window was black, like the glass was painted from the outside.
The driver never looked up. But when she tapped her card, he said, you're early. She wasn't.
She got off two stops early and walked home. That is why she is alive to tell this.
The next morning, three passengers from that same bus were reported missing. All of them stayed on until the last stop.
City records show route 33 was decommissioned in 1987. The bus that runs it now has no license plate.
The nurse still rides it sometimes. She says someone has to find out where the last stop is.
She has never made it past stop nine. Something always makes her pull the cord. Would you ride it? Comment 333.
My neighbor knocked on my door at 3 AM and said seven words I still cannot forget. Do not let it know you're home.
I laughed. He didn't. He was shaking, staring past me into my hallway.
He said for two weeks, something had been standing in my living room window every night. Watching him watch it.
I live on the fourth floor.
We both stood there in silence. Then his eyes went wide. He looked at my window. The curtains were moving.
I closed the door. I don't know why I closed the door. I locked myself in with it.
The knocking started five minutes later. Slow. Patient. It knew the rhythm of my heartbeat.
By sunrise it stopped. My neighbor's door was open. He was gone. He has never come back.
The police found his shoes outside my door, lined up perfectly, toes pointing at me. Have you ever heard knocking at 3 AM? Like this if you would have opened.
A mother in Ohio heard a voice on her baby monitor at 2 AM. It was not coming from the nursery.
It was coming from inside the monitor itself. And it was calling her name.
She ran to the nursery. Her daughter was asleep. The monitor on the crib was switched off.
But it was still transmitting. From the off state.
The voice said, she's fine. You're the one who should check your room.
She checked. The window was open. This is a third floor apartment. The lock was painted shut last summer.
She grabbed her daughter and slept in the car. In the morning, on the nursery wall, written in dust, it said, next time close the window.
The building has no record of anyone living above, below, or beside her corner unit. Would you have checked the room? Comment MOM if this got you.
A locksmith in Berlin received an order for one duplicate key. The order form was his own address.
His address. His door. His name, written in his own handwriting. He had not written it.
He assumed it was a prank, until he found a second key inside his own lock that evening. Brand new. Exactly the one he would have made.
He changed the locks that night. At 3 AM, someone tried the old key anyway. Then stopped.
Then a voice from the hallway said, calm and polite, it's okay. I have the new one.
He called the police. They arrived in four minutes. The hallway was empty. The doormat was still warm.
Weeks later, his doorbell camera caught one frame of a man holding a key up to the lens. Smiling.
The locksmith moved cities. Last month, he received another order form. One duplicate key. His new address, in his handwriting again.
He is moving again tonight. If you were him, would you make the key? Or would that be exactly what it wants? Like this if you would burn the order.
A family printed their vacation photos in 1996. In one picture, there is an extra person standing behind them.
Nobody remembers a stranger. Nobody in the photo is looking at him. But he is in focus. They are not.
The father zoomed in. The man is wearing the same shirt as him. The same watch. The same face.
It is him. Standing three feet behind himself. In a photo taken by a timer. Alone.
He burned the photo. That night, in every mirror of the house, a figure stood three feet behind whoever was looking.
They moved. The photo was gone. But last year, his daughter found the negative in a box marked do not develop.
She held it up to the light. In the image, the second father is closer now.
One foot behind. Still smiling. Still counting down the distance.
The family swears they will never develop it. But the negative is missing now. Would you have looked? Comment PHOTO.
A hotel in Chicago has an elevator with no button for floor 13. But sometimes, the elevator stops there anyway.
The doors open to a hallway identical to every other floor. Same carpet. Same lights. Except every door is room 13.
A businessman stepped out in 2011 on a dare from his colleagues. His room was 1313.
He said the room was normal. Perfect, even. Fresh towels. A mint on the pillow.
Then he noticed the window. It showed the lobby, thirteen floors down, from the wrong angle. Like he was looking up at himself.
He went back to the elevator and pressed 7. The doors opened to a wall of solid brick.
He says the brick was warm. And that something on the other side was knocking politely, in the same rhythm as his own heart.
Hotel staff found him at 5 AM, asleep in the elevator, holding a key card for room 1313. The hotel has no floor 13. No room 1313 exists. The key is real.
He still has it. It works on his front door at home. Would you have stepped out? Comment 13 if you felt that.
There is a forest in Poland where GPS stops working. Not weak signal. It stops. Like the satellites do not know it exists.
Hikers' phones freeze at the tree line and show one screen. No route found.
In 2018, a documentary crew drove in with a generator, film gear, and a satellite phone for backup.
The satellite phone connected on the first try. It called a number. Not the number they dialed.
A voice answered in Polish. Please leave. We can hear you.
They left. On the drive out, their footage showed the forest moving in the background of every shot. The trees getting closer with every take.
The crew published everything. The comments found one detail they had missed. In the final shot, standing between the trees, someone wearing their missing camera bag.
They never went back for the bag. The forest is on no map. The road to it does not appear in winter.
Would you drive in to check? Comment FOREST if you would stay on the road.
A woman kept her dad's final voicemail for six years. Last Tuesday, the message changed.
Same date. Same time stamp. Different voice. Deeper. Slower. And it knew things.
It said, you moved the couch. You painted the hallway gray. You stopped watering the plant he gave you.
All true. All things no voicemail from 2019 could know.
She played it for her sister. On her sister's phone, it was still the original. Happy birthday, sweetheart. Call me back.
Only her phone heard the new message. She checked the carrier. The voicemail server had no record of any update.
The message ends the same way every time now, but it adds one more word each week.
Last week it ended, call me back, please. This week, call me back, please, Maya.
She never told anyone her childhood nickname was Maya. Would you call the number back? Like if you got chills.
I noticed it on a Tuesday. The man in my bathroom mirror blinked half a second after I did.
I tested it for a week. Toothbrush up, he lagged. Hair down, he lagged. Every single time, half a second behind.
I told myself it was tired eyes, until the night he raised his hand when I had not.
Just a small wave. Almost polite. Like he was saying, finally, you noticed.
I covered the mirror with a towel. From behind the fabric, I heard breathing that matched mine, half a second late.
My roommate took the towel off as a joke. The mirror showed the bathroom. Empty. Behind him, a second man. Smiling.
We moved out that week. The new tenants posted online about a weird echo in the bathroom.
They said it feels like someone is always half a second away from copying you.
I still get tagged in their posts. I never reply. Would you have taken the towel off? Comment MIRROR if this one got you.
In 1954, the fishing town of Bellhaven in Scotland had 611 residents. Today, every official record lists it as zero. No one remembers it emptying.
The houses still stand. Doors unlocked. Meals set on tables. A kettle in every kitchen, still warm, according to the last survey team.
The team of four went in 1988. The survey paperwork lists them checking in at the harbor at 9 AM.
It lists them checking out at 9 AM. Same timestamp. Same morning. Their own writing.
None of them remember the years between. One woke up in a hospital three hundred miles away, with rope burns on both wrists.
He kept one thing from Bellhaven. A brass door key, warm to the touch. It is always warm. His doctor has no explanation.
In 2020, a drone flew over Bellhaven. On the thermal camera, every house radiated heat. Every single one. The chimneys were cold.
The drone's last frame shows 611 people standing in the streets, looking straight up at the camera. Perfectly still. Smiling.
The footage is real. The analysis is public. Would you walk those streets? Comment BELLHAVEN if you want part two.
A radio engineer in Nevada records dead air for quality checks. In 2021, his recorder caught a tower broadcasting back.
Every tower has a carrier hum. His recording had one too, until minute nine. Then the hum spelled letters in Morse.
It spelled his name. His full name. Including the middle name nobody has used since his mother died.
He checked the logs. The transmission came from tower seven. Tower seven was dismantled in 1996.
He played it for a colleague. His colleague heard only dead air. The name only plays for him.
Every night at 2:17, the hum returns. Each night, one new letter. He keeps a notepad by his bed.
The letters have spelled a sentence so far. We know you read it.
He does not know what it means. But he has stopped sleeping, because at 2:16, something knocks on the tower door. Politely. Then waits.
He records everything now and posts the audio. Listen with headphones. Would you open the tower door at 2:17? Comment TOWER.
A hiker in Norway got lost for six hours. When rescuers found him, they were not looking for him.
They were looking for the hiker who reported him missing. His own emergency call, placed two hours before he made it.
The call came from his phone. In his voice. It described his jacket, his route, his blood type.
The problem. He was still on the mountain, climbing, when that call went out.
The rescuers checked his call history with him. There was no record. Their system, though, had the full recording.
They played it in the rescue truck. His own voice, calm, said, I know you'll find him. But don't follow the footprints down.
The footprints led down. The team followed protocol and ignored them. Good. Something had pressed those prints deep. Eighty kilos heavier than him, by the depth.
They brought him down by a different path. In the truck mirror, the ridge was lined with figures standing, watching. The rescue photos show only rocks.
He hikes elsewhere now. Would you have followed the footprints? Like this if you trust protocol.
A morgue attendant in Chicago works alone at night. The rules on her first day were written by whoever held the job before her.
Rule one. If a drawer is open when you arrive, do not close it. Count the drawers first.
There are forty drawers. Some nights, she counts forty-one.
Rule two. On those nights, log the extra as visitor and go home early. Never look inside.
She followed the rules for two years. Then, last October, the extra drawer was already labeled. With her full name. In her handwriting.
She did not look. She went home. At 3 AM, her phone buzzed. The morgue's front desk number.
A calm voice said, you did well. That's why it's empty again.
She checked the morning count. Forty. Everything normal. Except the logbook entry she never wrote. Visitor left. Will return. In her handwriting.
She still works nights. She says whoever held the job before her is protecting her. Would you have looked in the drawer? Comment DRAWER if you would have followed the rules.
A museum archivist in Belfast was cataloging telegrams from 1912. One of them was addressed to her.
Her full name. On a telegram dated the night the Titanic sank.
The message read, stop searching the archive. Some messages arrive late.
She assumed an elaborate prank, until she found the sender's copy in the same box. In her own handwriting. Dated 1912.
The archive temperature log showed the box had been handled at 2:20 AM. By a staff badge that was decommissioned in 1978.
She pulled the badge photo. It was her face. Older. Tired. Wearing the museum's own archivist badge.
She applied for the night archive shift the next week. Her manager said the position had been filled. Since 1912.
On her last day, she found a second telegram. Same date. Two words. See you.
She still works days. The night archive door stays locked. But every April 14th at 2:20 AM, the corridor lights flicker once. Would you take the night shift? Comment 1912.
A cave diver in Florida mounted a camera on his helmet for a routine dive. The tape was recovered two hundred meters past the point of no return.
He was experienced. The passage was mapped. He had done it eleven times.
At minute six, his light caught a wall that is not on any map. Smooth. Carved. With handholds.
Handholds placed at diving depth, leading down. Someone made them. For divers.
His air was fine. He had a reason to turn back at minute eight. Instead, the camera shows him following the handholds down.
The last clear frame shows an opening. A dry cave, air above the water. And a wooden shelf with eleven helmets on it.
Eleven. Like his eleven previous dives. All accounted for. His garage has ten helmets. He could never find the one from his first dive.
The tape runs thirty more minutes in darkness. The audio is breathing. Two sets. One of them is his.
The dive community sealed that passage. Would you have followed the handholds? Comment DIVE if you would have turned back at minute eight.
My dog started barking at our living room wall every night at exactly 3:07. Not the door. Not a sound. The wall.
He would growl low, then bark three times. Then sit. Every night. 3:07. To the minute.
I checked the wall with a stud finder. Between two studs, there is a gap that reads as hollow. In a house with solid brick walls.
I drilled a small hole. The dog went silent for the first time in weeks. That scared me more than the barking.
Inside, I found nothing. No cavity. No space. Solid brick behind solid brick.
But the drill bit came out warm. And it came out shorter. Like something on the other side had eaten the metal.
I sealed the hole. The dog stopped barking at the wall. Now he barks at me. Only at me. Every night at 3:07.
My wife says I'm being paranoid. My dog agrees with her. That is the problem. My dog agrees with her, and my dog has not let her touch his food bowl since the wall.
We are staying at her mother's this week. I am not sure which of them I am worried about. Would you have drilled? Like if you would have sealed it too.
A travel blogger stayed at a hotel in Prague where the corridor has doors one through eight, then a wall, then doors ten through twenty.
No door nine. Not removed. Bricked over, from the corridor side. The outline is still visible under the paint.
On her second night, her key card demagnetized. The front desk gave her a new one. Room 9.
She laughed and said there is no room 9. The clerk went pale, checked the screen, and said, you checked in to 9 yesterday. You're in it now.
She walked to her door. It was her own room. Door 9, where door 7 should be. The paint outline was gone.
Inside, everything was hers, the way she had left it. Except her suitcase was unpacked. She never unpacks on the first night.
The bathroom mirror had a note written in steam. Welcome back. In her handwriting.
She checked out at 4 AM. The hotel has no record of room 9, and no outline under the paint anymore. Smooth wall. Like it never was.
Her review is still up. Clean rooms, friendly staff. Just don't unpack on the first night. Would you have stayed the night? Comment NINE if you want to know who unpacked.
There is a lake in Finland that stays liquid at minus forty. The locals don't skate on it. They don't fish. They don't look at it for long.
In 1979, a scientist measured its temperature. Constant. Every depth. Every season. Exactly four degrees. Like it is being kept that way.
He dropped a weighted camera down on a cable. At ninety meters, the water was not water anymore. The camera showed a ceiling.
A smooth ceiling, and below it, a room. With a table. And two chairs facing each other.
The cable kept feeding out. The reading said three hundred meters down. The lake bed map says the lake is twelve meters deep.
The camera's last frame. The two chairs. One of them had just been pushed back. Like someone stood up.
The cable snapped. Not cut. Snapped, from the bottom, upward. The lake has not given anything back since.
The scientist published his data and left the country. He said one thing in his final interview. The lake is not deep. It is above something deep.
The lake is fenced now. The fence has no gate. Would you have looked through the ice? Comment LAKE if this one stuck with you.
